sn6.10:6.1: Assuming that the _khārika_ (“bushel”) here is the _khāri_ of the Arthaśāstra, it is about 150 kg (Olivelle *King, Governance, and Law*, appendix 2, pg. 458; see also note on [sn3.13:1.2]()). Twenty bushels would be 3000 kg, which is reasonable; teams of bullocks regularly pull twice that amount. Estimating one gram of sesame having 500 seeds, a cartload would contain about 1,500,000,000 seeds. Removing one per century, it would take 150 billion years to empty (1.5 × 10¹¹). The number is multiplied nine times by twenty, so life in the Pink Lotus hell is 2.7 × 10¹³ years.
sn6.10:6.2: Ten hells are listed here, the names of which do not correspond with the 21 or 28 listed in Purāṇas, nor with the seven Jain hells, nor with the hells of [mn130](). The commentary offers three explanations for the obscure names of these hells: they are numbers reflecting the duration spent in Avīci; or they are the cries uttered by those suffering there; or they are simply the cold hells.
sn6.10:6.9: The _sogandhika_ is variously identified as blue or white.
sn6.10:10.1: The commentary here and to [an10.89]() specifies the large numbers in Pali as follows: _koṭi_ = 10⁷; _pakoṭi_ = 10¹⁴; _koṭipakoṭi_ = 10²¹; _nahuta_ = 10²⁸; _ninnahuta_ = 10³⁵; _abbuda_ = 10⁴²;  _nirabbuda_ = 2 × 10⁴³. The relations between the numbers in this passage are not clear, but if we follow the grammar suggested by Vanarata, they work out as follows (Bodhi, *Numerical Discourses*, footnote 626 to [an4.3:5.1]()). _Sataṁ sahassānaṁ nirabbudānaṁ chattiṁsatī_ is 136,000 × (2 × 10⁴³) = 2.72 × 10⁴⁸ (“2.72 quinquadecillion”). _Pañca sahassānaṁ ca abbudāni_ is 5000 × 10⁴² = 5 × 10⁴⁵ (“five quattuordecillion”). This is many orders of magnitude different from the 2.7 × 10¹³ which we calculated as the lifespan in the Pink Lotus hell. But the number here is the total number of years in multiple-hell rebirths, rather than the lifespan in a single hell. Also, it should go without saying, all such estimates of numbers are highly uncertain. The _abbuda_, for example, is said to be 10⁴² here, but Sanskrit sources put it variously at ten million, a hundred million, and ten billion.
